title: Electric current
body: I = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 11.1.A.1 "Current is the rate at which charge passes through a cross-sectional area of a wire."

title: Direction of conventional current
body: Conventional current is drawn in the direction positive charge would move, even though current in common circuits is actually due to moving electrons; schematics use conventional current unless otherwise specified.
caution: Current is not a vector. Its direction is tied to the motion of positive charge, not to any coordinate system.
ced_evidence: 11.1.A.2.i "The direction of conventional current is chosen to be the direction in which positive charge would move."; 11.2 boundary statement

title: Zero current means zero net motion of charge carriers
body: If the current in a section of wire is zero, the net motion of charge carriers is zero, although individual charge carriers still have nonzero speed.
caution: Do not say the charge carriers are stationary. Say the net motion is zero.
ced_evidence: 11.1.A.1.ii "the net motion of charge carriers in the wire is also zero, although individual charge carriers will not have zero speed"

title: Electromotive force (emf)
body: Emf (\mathcal{E}) is the electric potential difference that drives charge to move in a circuit; for a battery it is the potential difference the battery would supply if it were ideal, measured across its terminals when there is no current in the battery.
ced_evidence: 11.1.A.1.i "electromotive force, or emf"; 11.5.B.1.iii

title: Closed circuit
body: A closed circuit is one in which charges would be able to flow.
ced_evidence: 11.2.A.2.i "A closed circuit is one in which charges would be able to flow."

title: Open circuit
body: An open circuit is one in which charges would not be able to flow.
ced_evidence: 11.2.A.2.ii "An open circuit is one in which charges would not be able to flow."

title: Short circuit
body: A short circuit is one in which charges would be able to flow with no change in potential difference.
ced_evidence: 11.2.A.2.iii "charges would be able to flow with no change in potential difference"

title: Circuit schematic symbols
body: Standard symbols used to draw circuit schematics; a variable element has a diagonal strikethrough arrow across its standard symbol.

items.label: Switch
items.meaning: Opens or closes a path for charge

items.label: Variable element
items.meaning: Standard symbol with a diagonal strikethrough arrow

ced_evidence: 11.2.A.4.ii "Circuit elements have common symbols that are used to create schematic diagrams."

title: Resistance
body: Resistance is a measure of the degree to which an object opposes the movement of electric charge.
caution: Resistance belongs to an object. Resistivity belongs to a material.
ced_evidence: 11.3.A.1 "Resistance is a measure of the degree to which an object opposes the movement of electric charge."

title: Resistivity
body: Resistivity is a fundamental property of a material, depending on its atomic and molecular structure, that quantifies how strongly the material opposes the motion of electric charge; for a conductor it typically increases with temperature.
caution: Do not confuse resistivity with resistance. Resistivity does not depend on the object's length or cross-sectional area.
ced_evidence: 11.3.A.2.i; 11.3.A.2.ii "The resistivity of a conductor typically increases with temperature."

title: Resistance of a uniform resistor
body: R = \frac{\rho \ell}{A}
ced_evidence: 11.3.A.2 "proportional to its resistivity and length and is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area"

title: Ohm's law
body: I = \frac{\Delta V}{R}
ced_evidence: 11.3.B.1 "Ohm's law relates current, resistance, and potential difference across a conductive element"

title: Ohmic materials and the I–ΔV graph
body: Ohmic materials have constant resistance for all currents, and the resistance of an ohmic element is found from the slope of its graph of current versus potential difference.
caution: On a graph of I (vertical) versus ΔV (horizontal), the slope equals 1/R, not R.
ced_evidence: 11.3.B.1.i "Materials that obey Ohm's law have constant resistance for all currents"; 11.3.B.1.iv

title: Resistors convert electrical energy to thermal energy
body: Resistors can convert electrical energy to thermal energy, which may change the temperature of the resistor and its environment.
ced_evidence: 11.3.B.1.iii "Resistors can also convert electrical energy to thermal energy"

title: Electric power
body: P = I\,\Delta V
ced_evidence: 11.4.A.1 "depends on the current in the element and the electric potential difference across it"

title: Power in a resistor (derived forms)
body: P = I^{2}R = \frac{(\Delta V)^{2}}{R}
ced_evidence: 11.4.A.1 "Derived equations"

title: Bulb brightness follows power
body: The brightness of a bulb increases with the power it dissipates, so compare powers to predict relative brightness.
ced_evidence: 11.4.A.2 "The brightness of a bulb increases with power"

title: Series connection
body: In a series connection, any charge passing through one element must proceed through all elements in that connection, with no other path available, so the current in each element is the same.
ced_evidence: 11.5.A.1.i "The current in each element in series must be the same."

title: Parallel connection
body: In a parallel connection, charges may flow through one of two or more paths, and the potential difference is the same across each path.
ced_evidence: 11.5.A.1.ii "Across each path, the potential difference is the same."

title: Equivalent resistance in series
body: R_{eq} = \sum_i R_i
ced_evidence: 11.5.A.2.i "The equivalent resistance of a set of resistors in series is the sum of the individual resistances."

title: Equivalent resistance in parallel
body: \frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{R_i}
ced_evidence: 11.5.A.2.ii "The inverse of the equivalent resistance ... is equal to the sum of the inverses"

title: Adding parallel paths lowers equivalent resistance
body: When resistors are connected in parallel, the number of paths available to charges increases and the equivalent resistance of the group decreases.

title: Ideal batteries, wires, and meters
body: Unless otherwise stated, batteries, wires, and meters are assumed ideal. Ideal batteries have negligible internal resistance, and ideal wires have negligible resistance, which may be neglected only if the circuit contains other elements that do have resistance.
ced_evidence: 11.5.B.1, 11.5.B.1.ii; boundary statement "all batteries, wires, and meters are assumed to be ideal"

title: Terminal potential difference of a nonideal battery
body: \Delta V_{terminal} = \mathcal{E} - I r
caution: Model internal resistance r as a resistor in series with an ideal battery. The terminal potential difference is reduced only when there is current in the battery.
ced_evidence: 11.5.B.3 "the potential difference across the terminals of the battery is reduced"; 11.5.B.2

title: Ammeter connection
body: An ammeter measures current at a specific point and must be connected in series with the element being measured; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
ced_evidence: 11.5.C.1.i "Ammeters must be connected in series"; 11.5.C.1.ii

title: Voltmeter connection
body: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and must be connected in parallel with the element being measured; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance so no charge flows through it.
ced_evidence: 11.5.C.2.i "Voltmeters must be connected in parallel"; 11.5.C.2.ii

title: Nonideal meters change the circuit (qualitative only)
body: Nonideal ammeters and voltmeters change the properties of the circuit being measured, and AP Physics 2 expects only a qualitative discussion of how they affect measurements.
ced_evidence: 11.5.C.3 "Nonideal ammeters and voltmeters will change the properties of the circuit"; boundary statement

title: Energy change of a charge in a potential difference
body: \Delta U_E = q\,\Delta V
ced_evidence: 11.6.A.1 "charges moving through electric potential differences within circuit elements"

title: Kirchhoff's loop rule
body: \sum \Delta V = 0
caution: State that the loop rule follows from conservation of energy, and that the sum is taken around a single closed loop.
ced_evidence: 11.6.A.3 "the sum of potential differences across all circuit elements in a single closed loop must equal zero"; 11.6.A.2

title: Graph of electric potential versus position in a loop
body: A graph showing the electric potential at points in a circuit as a function of position within a loop.

items.label: Changes along the graph
items.meaning: Potential differences across each circuit element

items.label: End of loop
items.meaning: Net change in potential around the closed loop is zero

ced_evidence: 11.6.A.4 "graph of electric potential as a function of position within a loop"

title: Kirchhoff's junction rule
body: \sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}
caution: State that the junction rule follows from conservation of electric charge.
ced_evidence: 11.7.A.2 "total amount of charge entering a junction per unit time must equal the total amount of charge exiting"; 11.7.A.1

title: Equivalent capacitance in series
body: \frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{C_i}
caution: The series equivalent capacitance is less than the capacitance of the smallest capacitor.
ced_evidence: 11.8.A.1.i; 11.8.A.1.ii "less than the capacitance of the smallest capacitor"

title: Equivalent capacitance in parallel
body: C_{eq} = \sum_i C_i
ced_evidence: 11.8.A.1.iii "the sum of the individual capacitances"

title: Capacitors in series carry equal charge
body: By conservation of charge, each capacitor in series has the same magnitude of charge on each plate.
ced_evidence: 11.8.A.2 "each of the capacitors in series must have the same magnitude of charge on each plate"

title: RC time constant
body: \tau = R_{eq} C_{eq}
ced_evidence: 11.8.B.1.i "The time constant of an RC circuit is a measure of how quickly the capacitor will charge or discharge"

title: Meaning of one time constant
body: Charging: in one time constant the capacitor's charge rises from zero to about 63% of its final asymptotic value. Discharging: in one time constant the charge falls from fully charged to about 37% of its initial value.
ced_evidence: 11.8.B.1.ii "approximately 63 percent"; 11.8.B.1.iii "approximately 37 percent"

title: Charging capacitor: initial to final state
body: How an initially uncharged capacitor behaves from the moment it is placed in a circuit until steady state.

items.label: Immediately after connection
items.meaning: Uncharged capacitor acts like a wire; charge flows easily to the plates

items.label: While charging
items.meaning: Capacitor potential difference, plate charge, and stored energy change over time and asymptotically approach steady state; branch current also changes

items.label: After a long time (t >> τ)
items.meaning: Fully charged, with maximum potential difference and zero current in the capacitor's branch

caution: Describe these states qualitatively; no mathematical model with respect to time is expected.
ced_evidence: 11.8.B.2.i; 11.8.B.2.iv "zero current in the circuit branch"; boundary statement

title: Discharging capacitor: initial to final state
body: How a charged capacitor behaves from the start of discharge until steady state.

items.label: Immediately after discharge begins
items.meaning: Charge on the plates and stored energy begin to decrease

items.label: While discharging
items.meaning: Capacitor charge, potential difference, and branch current all decrease toward steady state

items.label: After a long time (t >> τ)
items.meaning: Capacitor and its branch may be modeled with steady-state conditions

caution: Describe these states qualitatively; no mathematical model with respect to time is expected.
